Responding to questions about Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, she described him as a senior and respected politician but said his recent statements appeared to reflect political frustration and resentment over being excluded from decision-making.

She suggested that the absence of the political role he expected in the current technocratic setup might also be contributing to his dissatisfaction. However, she said the government would welcome his constructive suggestions and guidance.

Regarding the Dir Colony tragedy in Peshawar, Bilour said investigations into the incident had been completed and a detailed report would soon be shared with the media. Inspections of government and private schools and seminaries across the province had identified 4,049 educational institutions requiring repairs and rehabilitation.

A comprehensive plan was being prepared to improve these institutions. Students from affected schools would be shifted to nearby government schools, with arrangements for class-wise adjustments and second shifts wherever necessary to ensure continuity of education.

She said a subcommittee was also examining the responsibilities of relevant departments and tehsil municipal administrations to determine whether negligence had occurred in building approvals, inspections and supervision.

On law and order, she said eight modern armoured vehicles had been handed over to the provincial police. A comprehensive plan to improve police infrastructure and operational capacity would be prepared within the next five to six weeks. Paying tribute to police personnel who had sacrificed their lives in the war against terrorism, she said providing modern equipment and resources to the force was the government's responsibility.

The adviser said internal irregularities in the Sehat Card programme were being examined, but there was no intention to discontinue or abolish it. The performance and administrative affairs of Medical Teaching Institutions (MTIs), along with the professional competence of their governing boards, would also be reviewed.

On the anti-encroachment campaign, she said illegal occupation of government land, green belts and drainage channels had to be eliminated to address Peshawar’s traffic and sewage problems. The operation was continuing without discrimination, and no one was being granted concessions on political or personal recommendations. Cleared areas would subsequently be rehabilitated and beautified for public use.

The advisor further added that sanitation services in Peshawar were improving, with cleaning staff working late into the night to remove accumulated waste. A comprehensive waste collection plan was also being developed, alongside measures to address shortages of manhole covers and dustbins.

Concluding, Bilour said the government’s vision was not merely a slogan but a commitment to good governance, institutional reforms, accountability, transparency and public service. She said the government would continue pursuing these priorities while protecting the province’s interests through responsible conduct and institutional procedures.

headline: Poorna Jagannathan joins Scott Foley in Hulu's political drama 'Young Americans'
description: Poorna Jagannathan joins Hulu's Young Americans pilot as a series regular, with Natalia Leite set to direct the drama
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
Actor Poorna Jagannathan has joined the cast of Hulu’s upcoming drama pilot Young Americans as a series regular, while filmmaker Natalia Leite has been selected to direct the project.

Jagannathan, known for her roles in Never Have I Ever and Hulu’s Deli Boys, will play Maya Washburn, a controversial senator and former close friend and political ally of the US President, played by Scott Foley. Her character’s son, portrayed by Sam Rechner, becomes romantically involved with the President’s daughter, played by Billie Boullet.

The political drama is set at Capitol Crest Academy in Washington, D.C., where the children of the country’s most influential families navigate teenage relationships and rivalries against the backdrop of their parents’ political ambitions. A forbidden romance between students from opposing political families threatens to intensify tensions, amid secrets, scandals and power struggles.

Jagannathan joins previously announced cast members Foley, Boullet, Rechner, Mia Isaac, Oscar Winter and Lauren Mei.

Leite, who previously directed episodes of Hulu’s Black Cake and worked on The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox, will direct the pilot. Her appointment reunites her with Bruce Miller, creator of The Handmaid’s Tale, who is also executive producing Young Americans.

The series comes from writers and executive producers Chris Hutton and Eddie O’Keefe. Miller and Priscilla Poriand are also executive producers through White Oak, while 20th Television is producing the pilot.

Jagannathan recently appeared in HBO’s Lanterns alongside Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler. Her other credits include Apple’s Wolfs, and she is set to appear in Apple TV’s crime drama Nocturne, premiering October 30.

headline: Mckenna Grace channels Lucy Gray Baird in archival Gucci for ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ photocall
description: The embroidered birds and snakes echoed the film’s themes, while the colourful skirt recalled Lucy Gray's dress
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
Mckenna Grace has continued her The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping press tour with another fashion tribute to the franchise, this time channeling Lucy Gray Baird in an archival Gucci gown.

The actress attended the film’s London photocall in a Gucci Fall 2016 gown designed by Alessandro Michele, featuring colourful bird embroidery, snake motifs and cascading ruffles that transition from green to pink.

The look was a deliberate reference to Rachel Zegler’s Lucy Gray Baird, the character introduced in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.

The gown’s embroidered birds and snakes echoed the earlier film’s themes, while its tiered, colourful skirt recalled the dress Lucy Gray wore during her performances. The nature-inspired details also connected with Sunrise on the Reaping, which features its own symbolism drawn from the natural world and the mockingjay.

Grace, who plays Maysilee Donner in the upcoming prequel, has been embracing the franchise’s fashion legacy throughout the film’s promotional tour. Working with stylist Molly Dickson, the actress has worn a series of outfits referencing characters, costumes and symbols from the Hunger Games films.

Her latest look also carried an unexpected connection to her co-star Elle Fanning.

Fanning previously wore the same Gucci Fall 2016 gown for a 2016 W Magazine editorial, although she did not wear it on the red carpet. The similar bird-embroidered Gucci Spring 2016 dress she wore to the 2015 Trumbo premiere had initially prompted the fashion comparison.

Grace’s archival Gucci appearance adds another carefully chosen reference to a press tour that has turned her wardrobe into a celebration of the franchise’s visual history.

headline: ‘Honey, that’s cheating’: Internet reacts to Kristen Bell’s explanation of Dax Shepard’s flirting
description: Bell explained that Shepard compliments strangers and that she interprets the gestures as flirting with her
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
Kristen Bell has sparked a debate online after revealing how her husband, Dax Shepard, flirts with her by complimenting other people, with some internet users questioning whether the unusual approach counts as flirting at all.

The actress discussed the couple’s relationship during an October 26 episode of Shepard’s Armchair Expert podcast, which featured her Nobody Wants This co-stars Adam Brody, Justine Lupe and Timothy Simons.

Bell explained that Shepard sometimes compliments people they encounter, including restaurant staff, and that she interprets the gestures as a way of expressing affection towards her.

“There’s a couple things Dax does where he doesn’t have to look up and wink at me, but I know that he’s just being the best boy,” Bell said.

She recalled Shepard complimenting a restaurant server by telling them they had “incredible eyelashes” and “gorgeous eyes”.

When podcast co-host Monica Padman suggested Shepard was flirting with the server, Bell disagreed, explaining that she viewed the interaction as a way of flirting with her instead.

“But that’s flirting with me, because he just made someone else feel good,” Bell said.

The actress added that Shepard was unlikely to have any further interaction with the person, describing the chance of him having another conversation with the server as “so microscopic”.

Bell said she interpreted her husband’s behaviour as affectionate because she saw him actively smiling at people and giving them compliments.

However, her explanation prompted mixed reactions online, with some users questioning the couple’s interpretation of flirting.

One commenter wrote, “Honey that’s cheating,” while another shared a GIF of Adele to express confusion over the couple’s relationship dynamic.

Others questioned whether the gesture could genuinely be considered flirting with a partner, with one user asking, “And this is considered flirting with your wife?”

Some commenters also expressed frustration at repeatedly encountering details about the couple’s marriage, while another joked, “Whatever that means. Let me stay out of straight people’s business.”

Bell and Shepard married in October 2013 and share two daughters, Lincoln and Delta. The couple have frequently spoken openly about their relationship, sharing personal anecdotes and unconventional conversations that have become a familiar part of their public image.

Bell’s latest comments have once again prompted online discussion about the couple’s dynamic, with reactions ranging from amusement to disbelief over her interpretation of Shepard’s compliments.

headline: Special audit targets JUI-F chief’s lands in K-P
description: Revenue board probes discrepancies in property tax payments
author: Ramzan Seemab
article_text:
Land transfers involving properties registered in the names of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman and his brothers — Maulana Lutafur Rehman, Attaur Rehman and Ziaur Rehman — have come under scrutiny after the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa Board of Revenue (BoR) ordered a special audit and verification of land records in Dera Ismail Khan and Paharpur over alleged irregularities.

The scrutiny stems from an official letter dated Oct 29, 2025, directing the Dera Ismail Khan deputy commissioner and district collector to conduct a detailed examination of property transfers, ownership documents and mutation registers relating to several properties in Abdul Khel, Shorikot and urban areas of the district.

The properties under scrutiny include a residential compound, a hujra (private chamber) and around 64 kanals of land in Abdul Khel; approximately 88 kanals of agricultural and 24 kanals of commercial land in Shorikot; and a residential and commercial property measuring 18 kanals and 12 marlas in urban DI Khan.

The audit observations have raised questions about land classification, oral mutations, declared property valuations, and payment of government dues. The document also highlighted discrepancies between declared and estimated property values, potentially resulting in short payments of stamp duty and Capital Value Tax (CVT).

The BoR has directed the district administration to take original land records and cadastral maps covering the period from 2002 to 2025 into safe custody. A precautionary entry is also to be recorded to prevent further transfers of the properties under investigation.

The authorities have further been asked to issue notices for recovery of any outstanding government dues and initiate departmental inquiries into the conduct of the revenue officials concerned.

Copies of the letter were also sent to the principal secretary to the chief minister, the director general of K-P National Accountability Bureau, the chief commissioner of the Federal BoR’s Regional Tax Office in DI Khan, the divisional commissioner, the director of land records and the tehsildars of DI Khan and Paharpur.

However, the allegations and audit observations have not been independently verified.

No response from the individuals concerned or details of a final inquiry or judicial determination were available.

headline: Netflix brings back 'Haunted Hotel' for season 3 with major promise from creator
description: Netflix renews 'Haunted Hotel' for season 3 after strong viewership, with the animated series set to return in 2027
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
Netflix has renewed its animated comedy series Haunted Hotel for a third season, with the upcoming instalment scheduled to premiere in 2027.

The streaming platform announced the renewal ahead of Halloween, following strong viewership for the supernatural series. According to Netflix, the show's second season debuted on the Global English TV Top 10 list, while its first season has accumulated more than 15 million views since its release in September 2025.

Created by Matt Roller, known for his work on Rick and Morty, Haunted Hotel follows a single mother attempting to manage the world's most haunted hotel. She runs the establishment alongside her ghost brother, two children and a demon trapped inside a young boy's body, while dealing with an expanding collection of ghosts, monsters and supernatural incidents.

The animated series features the voices of Will Forte, Eliza Coupe, Skyler Gisondo, Natalie Palamides and Jimmi Simpson.

Roller expressed his excitement about the renewal, promising viewers another season filled with supernatural adventures and comedy.

“I’m so excited to invite viewers back to the Undervale!” he said, adding that season three would feature the biggest, funniest, scariest and saddest stories the series has delivered so far.

Roller also serves as an executive producer alongside Chris McKenna, Rick and Morty co-creator Dan Harmon and Steve Levy. Erica Hayes, who has also worked on Rick and Morty, serves as supervising director.

Animation studio Titmouse is producing the series, with Chris Prynoski, Shannon Prynoski, Antonio Canobbio and Ben Kalina also serving as executive producers.

Netflix has not yet announced an exact release date for Haunted Hotel season three. The new season is expected to arrive sometime in 2027.

headline: KATSEYE’s Yoonchae Jeung named Dr.Jart+’s first North America brand ambassador
description: Yoonchae said skincare was an important part of looking after herself, particularly amid her busy schedule as a singer
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
KATSEYE member Yoonchae Jeung has been named Dr.Jart+’s first-ever North America brand ambassador, becoming the face of the Korean skincare brand’s latest Premium BB Cream campaign.

The 18-year-old South Korean singer will front the campaign for the Estée Lauder-owned beauty company, marking a new chapter in its efforts to connect its Korean skincare heritage with a global audience.

Dr.Jart+ said the partnership brings together the brand’s Korean roots and Yoonchae’s fresh perspective on beauty, individuality and self-expression.

The collaboration also continues the company’s history of working with Korean artists, including K-pop boy band Enhypen.

“Music, especially K-pop, has always been an important part of how Dr.Jart+ shows up in culture,” said Ye Jin Kim, the brand’s vice-president and global brand lead.

“We love collaborating with Korean artists to share our Korean roots with fans around the world.”

Yoonchae will promote the brand’s Premium BB Cream, a skincare and make-up hybrid product that has recently been reformulated with 2% niacinamide and glycerin.

The updated formula is designed to moisturise the skin while providing SPF 30 coverage and a natural glass-skin finish. The product is available in eight shades.

Speaking about the partnership, Yoonchae said skincare was an important part of looking after herself, particularly amid her busy schedule as a performer.

“I have always believed that taking care of my skin is a way of taking care of myself,” she said.

“No matter how busy my schedule gets, I love having a simple routine that makes me feel confident and comfortable in my own skin. Dr.Jart+ has always felt fun and innovative to me.”

KATSEYE was formed in 2024 and has gained international recognition with songs including Gabriela, Animal and Gnarly.

The group’s growing presence across music, fashion and beauty has helped its members become prominent figures in global pop culture.

Dr.Jart+ said Yoonchae’s influence across these areas, alongside her Korean heritage, made her a natural choice for the campaign.

The Premium BB Cream is available through Dr.Jart+’s website and selected retailers.

article_html:
KATSEYE member Yoonchae Jeung has been named Dr.Jart+’s first-ever North America brand ambassador, becoming the face of the Korean skincare brand’s latest Premium BB Cream campaign.

The 18-year-old South Korean singer will front the campaign for the Estée Lauder-owned beauty company, marking a new chapter in its efforts to connect its Korean skincare heritage with a global audience.

Dr.Jart+ said the partnership brings together the brand’s Korean roots and Yoonchae’s fresh perspective on beauty, individuality and self-expression.

The collaboration also continues the company’s history of working with Korean artists, including K-pop boy band Enhypen.

“Music, especially K-pop, has always been an important part of how Dr.Jart+ shows up in culture,” said Ye Jin Kim, the brand’s vice-president and global brand lead.

“We love collaborating with Korean artists to share our Korean roots with fans around the world.”

Yoonchae will promote the brand’s Premium BB Cream, a skincare and make-up hybrid product that has recently been reformulated with 2% niacinamide and glycerin.

The updated formula is designed to moisturise the skin while providing SPF 30 coverage and a natural glass-skin finish. The product is available in eight shades.

Speaking about the partnership, Yoonchae said skincare was an important part of looking after herself, particularly amid her busy schedule as a performer.

“I have always believed that taking care of my skin is a way of taking care of myself,” she said.

“No matter how busy my schedule gets, I love having a simple routine that makes me feel confident and comfortable in my own skin. Dr.Jart+ has always felt fun and innovative to me.”

KATSEYE was formed in 2024 and has gained international recognition with songs including Gabriela, Animal and Gnarly.

The group’s growing presence across music, fashion and beauty has helped its members become prominent figures in global pop culture.

Dr.Jart+ said Yoonchae’s influence across these areas, alongside her Korean heritage, made her a natural choice for the campaign.

The Premium BB Cream is available through Dr.Jart+’s website and selected retailers.

headline: DG ISPR says Pakistan ‘cautiously optimistic’ on Iran-US mediation, warns against spoilers
description: Says there is no bar on Iran joining defence pact; adding that Pakistan is not involved in the Yemen conflict
author: Reuters
article_text:
Pakistan’s military is “cautiously optimistic” about its mediation between Iran and the United States, its spokesman said on Friday in his ​first interview since a high-level delegation visited Tehran this week.

Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir — Pakistan's chief mediator in its efforts to ‌de-escalate the now eight-month-old Iran war — has been to Tehran twice this month, most recently on Monday alongside Saudi and Turkish officials.

“Why would the field marshal be going twice if it is not for some positivity? So yes, of course,” spokesman Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said when asked whether the trips were a positive sign.

Pact does not bar new members

“The word ​that we would use is always cautiously optimistic,” added Chaudhry, director general of Inter-Services Public Relations.

There were still "powerful spoilers and detractors," who believed ​conflict serves them, he added without naming them.

Speaking in the garrison city of Rawalpindi, where Pakistan's armed forces are headquartered, ⁠Chaudhry declined to say what was discussed or whether the United States had backed the trip.

Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief ​Ibrahim Kalin joined CDF Munir in Tehran on Monday.

The two countries signed a joint defence pact with Pakistan on August 7, saying an attack on any signatory will ​be treated as an attack on all.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement has taken on added significance as the Iran war has redrawn regional alliances and raised fears of a broader Middle East conflict.

While the three signatories say the agreement is aimed at collective deterrence and regional security, analysts see its evolution as closely tied to efforts by regional powers to manage ​the fallout from the Iran-US confrontation.

After Monday’s talks, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said regional security should be ensured by regional ​countries without foreign intervention.

The wording of the pact does not bar new members, Chaudhry said on Friday when asked whether Iran could join.

“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective ‌deterrence and ⁠regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.

Asked whether more Pakistani troops were being sent to Saudi Arabia under the agreement, Chaudhry said that would depend on the situation and the decision of both countries’ political leadership.

He said Pakistan was committed to defending Saudi Arabia and the holy sites of Makkah and Madina. "We are not part of the Yemeni conflict, which is an ​intra-Yemen conflict," he added.

Fighting between Saudi ​Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group ⁠has been reignited by the Iran conflict, stoking fears of a wider war.

Home front

On the home front, the federal government suspended the provincial government in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, led by jailed former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), on October 11 ​and detained Chief Minister Sohail Afridi.

The government had accused the provincial administration of failing to tackle militancy. The PTI ​rejected the allegations and ⁠says its government took part in counter-terrorism efforts. PTI leaders called the move a pretext to crush protests.

Asked if there would now be larger military-led campaigns in the province, Chaudhry said that was not how the army conducted counter-terrorism.

"Our counter-terrorism operations are based on what we call IBOs, intelligence-based operations... The tempo of the freedom of ⁠action of (those) ​IBOs will further increase," he said.

Independents backed by Khan’s PTI won the most directly elected seats ​in the February 2024 election but fell short of a majority. K-P was the only province controlled by Khan’s party.

Khan has been in jail since 2023, and his supporters see the ​military behind his imprisonment and the dismantlement of the PTI. The army denies involvement in politics.

headline: 'Dune' and 'Dune: Part Two' return to IMAX theatres with exclusive 'Dune: Part Three' sneak peek
description: The announcement comes as anticipation builds for Dune: Part Three, which will continue the story of Paul Atreides
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
The first two Dune films are set to return to IMAX theatres next month, giving fans another chance to experience Denis Villeneuve’s sci-fi saga on the big screen ahead of the highly anticipated third instalment.

Warner Bros has announced that Dune (2021) and Dune: Part Two (2024) will return to IMAX for a limited theatrical run beginning November 13. The screenings will also include an exclusive sneak peek of Dune: Part Three, which is scheduled to arrive in cinemas on December 18.

The two films will be shown as a double feature on November 13, while additional screenings of each film are planned from November 14 to 18.

Tickets for the re-releases go on sale on October 30 through Fandango, IMAX and participating cinema websites.

The announcement comes as anticipation builds for Dune: Part Three, which will continue the story of Paul Atreides following his rise to power on Arrakis.

Timothée Chalamet will return as Paul, alongside Zendaya as Chani. The upcoming film also features Robert Pattinson as Scytale, a new character described as a shape-shifting antagonist who seeks to overthrow Paul.

The cast includes returning stars Rebecca Ferguson, Florence Pugh, Javier Bardem and Anya Taylor-Joy, while Jason Momoa is also returning to the franchise. Momoa’s son, Nakoa-Wolf Momoa, will play Leto II Atreides, one of Paul and Chani’s twin children, with Ida Brooke playing Ghanima.

Directed by Villeneuve, the first Dune film was released in 2021 and earned six Academy Awards from 10 nominations. Its 2024 sequel grossed more than $700 million worldwide and won two Oscars.

The IMAX re-release offers audiences an opportunity to revisit the first two films before the story concludes with Dune: Part Three, which is scheduled to open in cinemas on December 18, 2026.

headline: Govt increases diesel price by Rs2.29, petrol remains unchanged until Nov 2
description: Diesel will cost Rs402.96 per litre for next three days, while petrol remains unchanged at Rs377.91
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The federal government on Friday increased the price of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs2.29 per litre while keeping the petrol price unchanged for the next three days.

According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, petrol will continue to be sold at Rs377.91 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs402.96 per litre from Oct 31 to Nov 2.

The latest revision comes a day after the government raised the price of diesel by 85 paisa per litre for Oct 29, taking its price above the Rs400 mark.

On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.

On September 13, PM Shehbaz announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.

Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.

Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.

On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.

Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.

Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.

Global geopolitical developments continue to pose significant risks. International oil prices are influenced by decisions taken by OPEC+, conflicts in the Middle East, sanctions on oil-producing nations, and disruptions in critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea. Any interruption in these supply chains can immediately increase crude oil prices and freight costs. Since Pakistan imports the majority of its petroleum requirements, these developments quickly translate into higher domestic fuel prices.

Oil prices jumped by more than 2 per cent on Friday, on pace for a fourth straight monthly gain, as a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and the US reiterated the possibility of renewing hostilities in Iran.

Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's crude, was up 2.37 per cent at $117.56 a barrel at 7.32pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, added 2.13 per cent to $104.17 a barrel.

The Yemeni army targeted Saudi Aramco in a massive wave of missile ​attacks, according to a media report.

Those reports of a new spate of attacks helped oil recoup some losses later in the session, said ​John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital.

Earlier, US Vice President JD Vance sought to revive peace negotiations by sending a ⁠letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the Wall Street Journal said on Wednesday, citing US officials and people familiar with ​the matter.

"Oil prices are under pressure today amid renewed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the conflict in the Middle East," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.

Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's crude, was up 2.37 per cent at $117.56 a barrel at 7.32pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, added 2.13 per cent to $104.17 a barrel.
The Yemeni army targeted Saudi Aramco in a massive wave of missile attacks, according to a media report.
Those reports of a new spate of attacks helped oil recoup some losses later in the session, said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital.

Earlier, US Vice President JD Vance sought to revive peace negotiations by sending a ⁠letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the Wall Street Journal said on Wednesday, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter.
"Oil prices are under pressure today amid renewed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the conflict in the Middle East," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said.

headline: Party Rock Anthem singer Lauren Bennett's cause of death revealed after inquest
description: An inquest has ruled Party Rock Anthem singer Lauren Bennett's death a suicide, following her passing at 36 in July
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
Singer Lauren Bennett, best known for featuring on LMFAO’s hit song "Party Rock Anthem", died by suicide, according to the findings of an inquest into her death, TMZ reported. She was 36.

New details about Bennett’s death, which occurred in July 2026, emerged on October 30. According to TMZ, her body was discovered by her husband, Kenny Wormald, and her father.

Bennett’s death was previously investigated by police in the United Kingdom, with authorities reportedly believing that she had taken her own life. The inquest has now confirmed the cause of death.

Following the singer’s passing, her father shared an emotional tribute on social media, revealing that she had experienced a severe reaction to a prescribed medication in the months before her death.

He also expressed disappointment with the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), alleging that his daughter had not received adequate care during a particularly difficult period.

Bennett rose to international recognition through her contribution to LMFAO’s 2011 chart-topping track "Party Rock Anthem". The song became a major global hit and featured her vocals alongside the electronic dance music duo.

She was also a member of the girl group G.R.L., which released music during the 2010s.

Her death prompted tributes from those remembering her contribution to the music industry. The latest findings provide further details about the circumstances surrounding the singer’s passing, following the investigation earlier this year.

Bennett’s death has also renewed attention on her father’s concerns about the medical treatment she received before her passing.

headline: The degree is a receipt
description: The degree is a receipt
author: Mansoor Raza
article_text:
For over a decade I have taught in three classrooms that never meet. At NED University, my students are mostly middle class. At SZABIST, they come from the upper-middle and upper strata. On weekends, at the Amna Shamima Foundation in Ghulam Zakariya Goth, I teach survey skills free of charge, to girls from low-income homes. Different fees, different futures, one shrug. Interest is abandoned the moment a subject turns difficult. Assignments arrive late, and when they arrive on time, they arrive hollow. At University after four years, the degree is treated as a receipt: proof that the fee was paid, not that anything changed. Call it laziness and you miss the point. The student who ignores an assignment will happily spend nine hours teaching himself video editing on YouTube. His disinterest is selective, which makes it a judgment, not a defect. Young people have run the numbers, and the classroom lost.

The degree is the entry ticket, but the key is connections, not merit. Studying hard begins to look like paying full fare on a train where everyone else rides free. He has not stopped being intelligent; he has become strategically cynical; the cynics are half right. Pakistan's labour market does reward networks. But a graduate with a connection and no skill is a guest, not a colleague, and the door that opened for him closes as quickly. The cynic is right about the entrance and wrong about the staying. Privilege fails in its own way. In elite institutions, a family business or an inherited network makes effort feel optional, and education becomes a finishing school, a social stage rather than an intellectual one. Where failure costs nothing, commitment has no logic.

In the Goth, the logic inverts. These girls have everything to gain, and the course is free, yet attendance wavers. Look closer and the cause is not attitude but architecture. A family relocates for work, and a girl vanishes from the register. A marriage is arranged, and her stitching machine falls silent. A brother's schedule, a neighbour's gossip, harassment on the road to class: something decides whether she may leave the house, and it is rarely her. Her unfinished assignment is not defiance. It is the visible edge of a life in which she does not own her calendar. Deadlines presume autonomy, and autonomy is exactly what she lacks. One group is excused from effort by privilege, the other excluded from continuity by precarity, and both land in the same statistic: the dropout, the late submission, the half-finished skill.

Inflated grades turned marks into currency rather than evidence. Teachers who overlook plagiarism for the sake of peace taught that rules bend. A generation raised on cheating scandals, leaked papers and self-financed schemes learned early that the system is negotiable. We now demand integrity from students whose institutions never modelled it. Add an economy of thirty-second rewards, and a semester-long project paying off years later seems absurd.

The result is credential inflation without competence. Degrees multiply while capability thins. Employers, distrusting degrees, demand references, which feeds the very connection economy students already believe in. Meanwhile, girls who leave skill programmes early drift back into dependency, and a community loses its most plausible exit from poverty, one stitched seam at a time.

Make merit visible through public portfolios, live projects and employer-evaluated work, so that skill can be seen to beat introduction. Shorten the distance between effort and reward with modular certificates and early wins. Bring flexibility to the Goth: home-based tasks, mobile learning and conversations with fathers and brothers, so that permission becomes partnership. And let teachers become what the system is not: consistent, fair and incorruptible in small things.

If we want students to treat education as transformation, we must first make transformation worth more than the receipt. Until then, our classrooms will keep filling with bodies and emptying of learning.

headline: Deadlock and diplomacy
description: Deadlock and diplomacy
author: editorial
article_text:
With the Middle East on tenterhooks anticipating a new round of US-Israeli strikes on Iran, President Trump has further compounded the equation through his ambiguous stance on a plausible diplomatic initiative in the region. A battered White House incumbent, apparently staring down a projected defeat in the midterm polls, once again raised the stakes by expressing hope that the war with Iran would end soon - though he did not say how. He did, however, voice optimism that the Islamic Republic would not cross the nuclear threshold, hinting at behind-the-scenes maneuvering as Doha diplomats returned to Tehran with a message from Washington.

The diplomatic push got a shot in the arm as Vice President JD Vance also sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei, in an earnest endeavour to revive stalled negotiations. Though Tehran is yet to respond officially, it issued a diplomatic rejoinder at the UNSC, where its representative, Gholamhossein Darzi, condemned the US and Israel for their military aggression. Darzi blamed the duo for an illegal naval blockade, terming it the root cause of maritime insecurity in the Persian Gulf.

headline: Innovation against the odds
description: Innovation against the odds
author: editorial
article_text:
Pakistan's commendable position in a recent ranking of innovation outputs is a quiet but telling illustration of the country's potential. Pakistan rose to 95th in the Global Innovation Index 2026, regaining "overperformer" status in the World Intellectual Property Rights Organisation's ranking of 139 economies. While the number may not seem high, it is a relative grade, illustrating how Pakistan generates far more innovation than its meagre inputs - we were 121st in innovation inputs, but 72nd in outputs.

That gap is a tribute to the talent, hustle and resourcefulness of Pakistani inventors and entrepreneurs. The strengths are also concrete and market-driven. Pakistan ranks 10th globally in mobile-app creation relative to GDP, 15th in ICT services exports and 19th in high-tech imports. Each of these numbers reflects a generation that has managed to do well despite creaky infrastructure, patchy policy and limited state support. At the same time, it also shows why local talent wants to leave - they are too good for what Pakistan has to offer them.

After all, the same Innovation Index also places Pakistan near the bottom on human capital, research and infrastructure. R&D spending is just 0.16% of GDP, patent filings lag badly, and startup funding - which was already miserly by international standards - has crashed. For the government, the "overperformer" label should be seen as an insult, not an achievement. Output strength cannot indefinitely compensate for input neglect. Pakistani innovators deserve more. The state must be willing to meet them halfway, either by directly funding more research or creating the conditions for investors to come in. Investment-related laws also need work to ensure that they are no longer avenues for shady lending, but do encourage honest, calculated risk-taking. Only then will Pakistan's innovators be able to achieve more, while also reflecting well on what their country did for them.

headline: Healthcare for all
description: Healthcare for all
author: editorial
article_text:
The revival of the Pakistan-China Friendship Hospital in Islamabad under a public-private partnership is a welcome development, particularly at a time when affordable medical treatment remains beyond the reach of millions of Pakistanis. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's announcement that the government will bear the entire cost of treatment at the 182-bed facility, to be managed by the Indus Hospital and Health Network, offers a much-needed example of how public resources can be utilised for the welfare of ordinary citizens. Yet, while such partnerships deserve appreciation, they also expose the sorry state of Pakistan's healthcare system, which remains in complete disarray.

The reality is that healthcare in Pakistan has increasingly become a privilege rather than a fundamental right. Public hospitals are overwhelmed by patients, understaffed and frequently deprived of essential medicines and functioning equipment. Those who cannot secure timely treatment at government facilities are left at the mercy of private hospitals, where treatment can cost more than an ordinary household earns in several months. For countless families, a serious illness means exhausting their savings or selling whatever assets they possess. Many are compelled to delay treatment until their condition becomes critical, while others simply surrender to illnesses that could have been treated had they possessed the financial means.

The government's partnership with the Indus Hospital and Health Network demonstrates that quality treatment can be provided without charging patients. However, the provision of free healthcare cannot remain confined to a handful of institutions or depend indefinitely on charitable organisations and private management. It must become the guiding principle of national health policy. No individual should be denied treatment because of an inability to pay, nor should a family's financial circumstances determine whether a patient lives or dies.

headline: Reforming political parties: now!
description: Reforming political parties: now!
author: M Zeb Khan
article_text:
In my October 24 piece, I argued that political parties are caught between dynastic hangover and structure-less passion. Here, I will try to explain why they need reform and why now. Pakistan does not lack political passion. It lacks political institutions capable of converting that passion into durable democratic power. Every crisis produces familiar calls for unity, sacrifice and loyalty. Yet a party that can function only while its founder issues instructions has confused devotion with organisation. To withstand pressure from powerful unelected institutions, parties must first stop reproducing miniature authoritarian systems inside themselves.

The starting point is simple: a political party belongs to its members, not to a family, financier, founder or collection of social-media celebrities. Membership must mean more than filling rallies, defending a leader and waiting for instructions. It must confer enforceable rights to vote, question, contest office and demand explanations. Pakistan does not need to invent the principle. The Elections Act 2017 already requires party councils, general meetings and periodic intra-party elections. But holding a ceremonial vote is not democracy. Parties need independently maintained membership registers, genuine competition for offices, transparent results and impartial appeals against manipulation.

Next comes the right to dissent. An organisation that expels critics for disagreeing with leadership cannot credibly claim to champion freedom outside it. Equally, freedom cannot mean that every disagreement becomes an online trial and every rival a traitor. Parties need elected policy councils, formal grievance procedures, recorded decisions and defined protections for whistleblowers. Members should be free to criticise decisions, while those exercising authority should be accountable through agreed rules.

Leadership succession is another test. A founder's imprisonment, illness, retirement or death should trigger constitutional procedures, not a scramble among relatives, favourites and competing microphones. A credible deputy, empowered committees and published lines of responsibility allow an organisation to act without endlessly invoking the absent leader's presumed wishes.

The digital sphere needs reform too. Influencers have helped widen access to political debate, challenge gatekeepers and expose uncomfortable questions. But followers and algorithms are not substitutes for a membership mandate. Parties should publish timely explanations of strategic decisions, hold open question sessions and correct misinformation transparently.

Then comes the neglected question of who gets to rise. An ordinary worker should be able to progress from ward organiser to district leader to national policymaker without a wealthy sponsor or famous surname.

Money matters. When a party depends on a handful of patrons, its independence is only as strong as their willingness to resist pressure. Broad membership contributions, lawful small donations, audited accounts and disclosure of major funding interests would make political organisations more accountable to their supporters and less vulnerable to elite bargaining.

But internal reforms alone will not defeat coercion. Even the best-run party can be damaged by arrests, restrictions and suppression of peaceful activity. Pakistan therefore needs a constitutional understanding across rival parties: no political organisation should seek unelected intervention against a competitor, and every party's right to organise, contest elections and obtain due process must be defended irrespective of who benefits.

Finally, parties must become schools of citizenship. Local branches should debate budgets, oversee public services and prepare members for local government. Democracy is learned through the ordinary work of listening, negotiating and accepting defeat - not only through speeches about resistance. The real measure of reform is not whether a party can mobilise a crowd for its leader. It is whether members can peacefully replace that leader, survive external pressure and continue serving citizens. Pakistan will have stronger democracy when its parties stop asking people to protect personalities and begin giving them institutions worth protecting.

headline: The dark one's due
description: The dark one's due
author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
article_text:
Two revelations have jolted the Indian establishment. Former Supreme Court Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul alleges in his memoir that former Chief Justice DY Chandrachud was too deferential to the Modi government, even withdrawing cases that questioned the executive's delay in judicial appointments. That is a polite way to say he was compromised and in turn compromised the judiciary. An Indian Express report exposed how two Election Commissioners (a majority) were bypassed during the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Why the surprise? For twelve years the Modi-Shah-Doval nexus has left breadcrumbs mapping a creeping, hostile takeover of the republic.

The blueprint was written in the blood and silence of the Judge BH Loya case. In 2014 the judge hearing the Sohrabuddin fake encounter case, which implicated Amit Shah, died in suspicious circumstances. Whistleblowers revealed heavy pressure and bribery attempts from within the higher judiciary. The institutional burial of the case warned every courtroom in the country. It proved the state machinery would now whitewash street thugs, while institutional bigwigs eagerly sold their constitutional mandates for a few creature comforts. Whether a post-retirement Rajya Sabha seat for a compliant Chief Justice (Ranjan Gogoi), or a lucrative corner plot for a former Army Chief (VK Singh) who would practically drive his institution into the ruling party's lap to become a junior minister, the price of subverting a democracy was cheap. These fragile egos sold themselves for pennies on the pound.

Once the judiciary was tamed, the rot spread through the hard power structures. As early as 2015, prosecutor Rohini Salian told NDTV's Sreenivasan Jain of instructions from the National Investigation Agency leadership to go soft on right-wing terrorists in the Malegaon case. When I reminded you of this last year, the website of the channel, since taken over by Adani, which had evaded the ban on Indian news in Pakistan, was quickly banned. In 2016 the government bypassed the hallowed seniority principle to appoint General Bipin Rawat as Army Chief. The man would soon find his twin in Pakistan. Ideological alignment, sycophancy and expedience would henceforth trump institutional norms. The compromise is so absolute that the Army now mines ancient Indian texts for strategy under Project Udbhav, and the Integrated Defence Staff hails a Gita lecture to mid-level officers as inspiring.

The Central Bureau of Investigation was decapitated in a midnight executive coup removing Director Alok Verma and Special Director Rakesh Asthana to shield defence contracts like the Rafale purchase from scrutiny. In 2018 four Supreme Court judges, Justices J Chelameswar, Ranjan Gogoi, Madan B Lokur and Kurian Joseph, held an unprecedented mutiny, warning that democracy was at stake due to selective case assignments. The Reserve Bank of India and the Election Commission were overruled on the opaque Electoral Bonds scheme. When Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa dissented against clean chits for the ruling duo, state financial agencies hunted his family.

Capturing reality means capturing data. In early 2019 two acting members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest as the government buried their verified report showing unemployment at a 45-year high. It was leaked to Business Standard. Border realities were similarly hidden until last week, when Indo-Tibetan Border Police Director General Shatrujeet Kapur confirmed ongoing military face-offs with Chinese troops in the territory India administers as Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as South Tibet (Zangnan), exposing the hollowness of the secure border story. After the 2019 Pulwama tragedy, former Governor Satya Pal Malik claimed the Prime Minister and the National Security Advisor told him to stay quiet about intelligence failures, proving that institutions were forced to guard political optics over soldiers' lives. That optic would lead to Modi's re-election and the abolition of Article 370.

The soft power pipeline was choked as ruthlessly. The first move tested the waters with blatant appointments, packing historical research councils with revisionists. The state then installed RSS enforcers as university vice-chancellors to break student resistance. It weaponised anti-terror laws in the Bhima Koregaon case, inventing the phantom threat of the urban Naxal to criminalise scholars like Anand Teltumbde, Sudha Bharadwaj, Shoma Sen and Hany Babu. Global academics like Romila Thapar met petty bureaucratic humiliation, forced to submit her curriculum vitae to a captured committee to prove her worth. Private sanctuaries fell when billionaires caved to government pressure, forcing critics like Pratap Bhanu Mehta out of Ashoka University. The goal was simple: to ensure the next generation lacked the historical vocabulary to question the Vishwa Guru project.

It is welcome that functionaries are finally speaking openly, even if only from the safety of retirement. It looks as though the deal Narendra Modi cut with the dark one for twenty-five years of unchecked power is drawing to a close, and his soul is ready to be collected. His recent manoeuvres fail to land with their old impact. The cracks are widening, and the leaks will only grow. Buckle up for far more shocking revelations.

This raises a terrifying question. When Modi's detractors finally replace him, how will they undo this staggering damage? The blueprint began years ago with Ajit Doval's pitch at Sastra University, where he argued for a ten-year unbroken term to rewire the Indian state. To decontaminate the system, the opposition must pitch for no less. Five years is not enough to dig out the ideological rot embedded by the lateral entry scheme and the unaccountable super-bureaucracy of the National Security Council Secretariat. By parachuting ideologically aligned individuals into Joint Secretary roles, the RSS has bypassed the rigorous UPSC examination, altering the genetic makeup of the civil service so the machinery stays loyal to the saffron agenda long after governments change.

The incoming leadership must also rethink its tools of restoration. The Congress party traditionally prefers polite diplomats from the Indian Foreign Service for the NSA post. But the intelligence community, the true muscle of the deep state, is largely made up of Indian Police Service officers. A diplomat cannot dismantle a hardened police state. You need a policeman who knows where the bodies are buried and how the truncheon is wielded: an officer unaffected by Ajit Doval's sprawling influence, with the moral clarity, motive and institutional memory to serve as the ultimate wrecking ball.

headline: Pakistan and Bangladesh: bitter past, and present
description: Pakistan and Bangladesh: bitter past, and present
author: Imtiaz Gul
article_text:
Nations in transition, such as Bangladesh, face a difficult choice. Burdened by a bitter past and a turbulent present, they must decide whether to hold everyone accountable while protecting human rights or move on in the interest of political and economic stability. The former risks drawing the country into a cycle of political revenge. The latter runs counter to the aspirations of those who struggled against an oppressive regime. This is a major test for the new government: can Bangladesh move beyond personalised autocracy towards democratic governance that people consider legitimate, in the context of the "student revolution" of summer 2024?

The leaders of this revolution, along with many others across the political and social spectrum, refuse to forget the brutal victimisation and persecution of opposition politicians, media professionals, intellectuals and human rights defenders during Hasina's rule, often with the active support of her loyalists at various levels.

This also raises the question of whether Prime Minister Tarique Rehman and his supporters can reduce the civil-military bureaucracy's hold over the political economy as they pursue their reform agenda. Addressing the deeply rooted interests and legacy of the Awami League is a major challenge in an environment marked by political divisions and polarisation.

Tensions remain high in an environment that often turns hostile. This was reflected in the strong remarks made by Nahid Islam, convener of the National Citizen Party (NCP) and opposition Chief Whip, during a media interaction on October 28.

"If we let this government off the hook, we may have to face another fascism. We do not want to have to overthrow another fascist regime at the cost of 1,400 lives again," warned Nahid Islam. He levelled several allegations against the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), saying that "the judiciary remains under the control of those in power, the (criminal) justice system has not been reformed, violence is rampant and the BNP-backed cadres are killing even their own party members" to settle personal scores.

In a reminder of the situation surrounding Pakistan's ruling elites, Nahid Islam also described Bangladesh as a "mafia state".

"Terrorists are armed, ministers and state ministers are also carrying weapons and this is what is called a mafia state," he said, accusing the authorities of failing to arrest "godfathers of the (drug) trade, members of drug syndicates and political leaders linked to the business."

These allegations may sound like an exaggerated charge sheet from a party that claims to represent the youth. However, their central concerns are difficult to dismiss and are common in countries undergoing political transitions. Islam's remarks reflect growing doubts about whether Bangladesh's post-uprising transition is producing meaningful reforms in law enforcement, the judiciary and democratic governance. The central argument of NCP members is that replacing one government is not enough if political patronage, violence, impunity and institutional weaknesses persist.

These concerns were clearly visible in discussions with Bangladeshi veterans and youth representatives during and on the sidelines of the recent annual Bay of Bengal conference. While geopolitics, interstate conflicts, the Iran-US-Israel war and the weakening of the UN-based global order dominated the proceedings, Bangladesh's domestic political and social situation and its foreign relations also featured prominently in various sessions.

One of the major challenges facing Prime Minister Rehman is navigating the complex relationship between Pakistan and India. While many Bangladeshis, both inside and outside the government, want a fresh chapter in relations with Pakistan, the legacy of Hasina's rule and the Awami League's traditionally pro-India position remain obstacles to these aspirations.

Bangladesh's foreign policy is gradually evolving, with a stated intention to engage with all regional countries. Dhaka is seeking broader engagement with China, Pakistan and the United States while maintaining a workable relationship with India. Its dependence on external trade and water supplies also leaves it vulnerable to sudden changes in US trade and aid policies.

Since the summer of 2024, Pakistan has reached out to Bangladesh to regain some of the diplomatic ground it had lost to India. Several diplomatic, defence and education-related initiatives have marked this effort, and a series of visits at different levels appears to have been well received. However, changing the deeply rooted pro-India mindset within the civil-military bureaucracy and governance structures will not be easy. The current government appears aware of these constraints and is therefore proceeding cautiously in its dealings with Pakistan. India, which surrounds Bangladesh on much of its land border and lies upstream of the country's major rivers, remains a major concern.

That is why the present government is keen to focus on fixing its internal socio-economic problems and moderating the political toxicity (calls for accountability of the Hasina era brutalities) while trying to integrate partnerships with China, India and Pakistan without antagonising any regional power.

article_html:
Nations in transition, such as Bangladesh, face a difficult choice. Burdened by a bitter past and a turbulent present, they must decide whether to hold everyone accountable while protecting human rights or move on in the interest of political and economic stability. The former risks drawing the country into a cycle of political revenge. The latter runs counter to the aspirations of those who struggled against an oppressive regime. This is a major test for the new government: can Bangladesh move beyond personalised autocracy towards democratic governance that people consider legitimate, in the context of the "student revolution" of summer 2024?

The leaders of this revolution, along with many others across the political and social spectrum, refuse to forget the brutal victimisation and persecution of opposition politicians, media professionals, intellectuals and human rights defenders during Hasina's rule, often with the active support of her loyalists at various levels.

This also raises the question of whether Prime Minister Tarique Rehman and his supporters can reduce the civil-military bureaucracy's hold over the political economy as they pursue their reform agenda. Addressing the deeply rooted interests and legacy of the Awami League is a major challenge in an environment marked by political divisions and polarisation.

Tensions remain high in an environment that often turns hostile. This was reflected in the strong remarks made by Nahid Islam, convener of the National Citizen Party (NCP) and opposition Chief Whip, during a media interaction on October 28.

"If we let this government off the hook, we may have to face another fascism. We do not want to have to overthrow another fascist regime at the cost of 1,400 lives again," warned Nahid Islam. He levelled several allegations against the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), saying that "the judiciary remains under the control of those in power, the (criminal) justice system has not been reformed, violence is rampant and the BNP-backed cadres are killing even their own party members" to settle personal scores.

In a reminder of the situation surrounding Pakistan's ruling elites, Nahid Islam also described Bangladesh as a "mafia state".

"Terrorists are armed, ministers and state ministers are also carrying weapons and this is what is called a mafia state," he said, accusing the authorities of failing to arrest "godfathers of the (drug) trade, members of drug syndicates and political leaders linked to the business."

These allegations may sound like an exaggerated charge sheet from a party that claims to represent the youth. However, their central concerns are difficult to dismiss and are common in countries undergoing political transitions. Islam's remarks reflect growing doubts about whether Bangladesh's post-uprising transition is producing meaningful reforms in law enforcement, the judiciary and democratic governance. The central argument of NCP members is that replacing one government is not enough if political patronage, violence, impunity and institutional weaknesses persist.

These concerns were clearly visible in discussions with Bangladeshi veterans and youth representatives during and on the sidelines of the recent annual Bay of Bengal conference. While many Bangladeshis, both inside and outside the government, want a fresh chapter in relations with Pakistan, the legacy of Hasina's rule and the Awami League's traditionally pro-India position remain obstacles to these aspirations.

Its dependence on external trade and water supplies also leaves it vulnerable to sudden changes in US trade and aid policies.

Several diplomatic, defence and education-related initiatives have marked this effort, and a series of visits at different levels appears to have been well received. However, changing the deeply rooted pro-India mindset within the civil-military bureaucracy and governance structures will not be easy. The current government appears aware of these constraints and is therefore proceeding cautiously in its dealings with Pakistan. India, which surrounds Bangladesh on much of its land border and lies upstream of the country's major rivers, remains a major concern.

That is why the present government is keen to focus on fixing its internal socio-economic problems and moderating the political toxicity (calls for accountability of the Hasina era brutalities) while trying to integrate partnerships with China, India and Pakistan without antagonising any regional power.

headline: LPG hits Rs550/kg as price spiral deepens
description: LPG hits Rs550/kg as price spiral deepens
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Karachi consumers are being squeezed by another sharp surge in LPG prices, with the per-kilogram rate jumping Rs50 in just a day to Rs550, nearly double the official price, as disrupted Iranian supplies fuel a deepening shortage and leave households with little choice but to pay through the nose for cooking gas.

Market sources said Iranian LPG supplies were failing to reach Karachi's markets, creating a shortage that local marketing companies were allegedly exploiting to push up prices at their discretion.

They attributed the disruption to difficulties in LPG imports from Iran, warning that the resulting supply gap was driving consumers towards increasingly expensive local supplies.

Shopkeepers said marketing companies were supplying LPG at inflated rates, severely affecting their businesses. The latest price surge has led to a decline of up to 50 per cent in sales, they added.

Consumers, meanwhile, said the absence of piped natural gas in their homes had made purchasing expensive LPG unavoidable. The escalating cost of cooking gas was putting additional pressure on household budgets and also threatening to push up transport fares, tandoor prices and bakery products.

Market sources warned that the situation could deteriorate further if Iranian supplies failed to return to normal and the government did not strengthen its oversight of LPG prices.

With winter approaching, Karachi faces the prospect of a worsening gas shortage and another round of price increases.

headline: Man held for Rs4.45m matrimonial scam
description: Man held for Rs4.45m matrimonial scam
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
What began with the promise of marriage and a new life in the United States allegedly ended in financial deception and blackmail for a Karachi woman, who was reportedly swindled out of Rs4.45 million by a man she met through a matrimonial website.

The suspect allegedly won the woman's confidence by promising to marry her and take her to the US before persuading her to transfer millions of rupees. He later allegedly used her private videos to blackmail her.

A judicial magistrate on Friday handed over the suspect, identified as Hussam Kazmi, to the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) on six-day physical remand in the case. The accused was produced before the court by NCCIA officials, where the IO informed the court that the suspect assured the woman that they would marry and subsequently move to the US. Using this pretext, he allegedly received a total of Rs4.45 million from her. The suspect later blackmailed the woman using her private videos.

Preliminary investigations have also suggested that the suspect may have targeted other women using a similar modus operandi.

headline: Probe into 'Rs7.5b KMC irregularities' sought
description: Probe into 'Rs7.5b KMC irregularities' sought
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Billions of rupees are reportedly being spent on Karachi's development, yet broken roads, inadequate civic facilities and unpaid pensions remain part of the mega city's everyday reality.

Against this backdrop, Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) Deputy Parliamentary Leader Taha Ahmed Khan has called for an investigation into alleged financial irregularities in the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC), seeking scrutiny of billions of rupees allocated for development schemes.

In a letter to Public Accounts Committee (PAC) Chairman Nisar Khuhro, Taha, who is also a PAC member, demanded an investigation into the utilisation of Rs7.5 billion earmarked for 188 KMC development schemes.

He also called for transparency in development tenders worth Rs15 billion to Rs16 billion issued during the current financial year and sought an inquiry by the Chief Minister's Inspection Team (CMIT) into KMC development schemes and the tendering process. Taha said alleged irregularities and interference in the award of development contracts should be investigated, claiming that assertions about billions of rupees being spent on development projects remained confined to official documents. He alleged that development projects were being used to benefit select individuals at the expense of public money.

Against this backdrop, Muttahida Qaumi Movement-Pakistan (MQM-P) Deputy Parliamentary Leader Taha Ahmed Khan has called for an investigation into alleged financial irregularities in the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC), seeking scrutiny of billions of rupees allocated for development schemes.

In a letter to Public Accounts Committee (PAC) Chairman Nisar Khuhro, Taha, who is also a PAC member, demanded an investigation into the utilisation of Rs7.5 billion earmarked for 188 KMC development schemes.

He also called for transparency in development tenders worth Rs15 billion to Rs16 billion issued during the current financial year and sought an inquiry by the Chief Minister's Inspection Team (CMIT) into KMC development schemes and the tendering process. Taha said alleged irregularities and interference in the award of development contracts should be investigated, claiming that assertions about billions of rupees being spent on development projects remained confined to official documents. He alleged that development projects were being used to benefit select individuals at the expense of public money.

headline: Home at last: 11 fishermen reunite with families
description: Home at last: 11 fishermen reunite with families
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Some homecomings are measured not in miles travelled, but in years of longing finally coming to an end. For 11 Pakistani fishermen returning from Indian prisons, the journey back to Karachi was one such moment. At the Edhi Centre in Tower, anxious waiting gave way to tearful embraces, garlands and showers of flower petals as families welcomed home those whose safe return they had prayed for over the years.

The fishermen, among 14 Pakistanis released from Indian custody, arrived in Karachi after being transported from the Wagah border in Lahore. As they arrived, family members struggled to hold back their emotions as years of separation gave way to joyous reunions.

According to an Edhi Foundation spokesperson, arrangements for the fishermen's free transportation to Karachi were made on the instructions of Foundation Chairman Faisal Edhi, who also bore all travel expenses.

Among those returning were six fishermen from Maripur - 28-year-old Muhammad Sharif Bengali, 35-year-old Noorul Amin Bangal, Kamal Hussain Bengali and Noor Nabi Bengali, 36-year-old Ameer Hussain Bengali, and 41-year-old Azeemuddin Bengali. They had been imprisoned in India since August 19, 2019.

Two other fishermen, 30-year-old Ahmed Noor and 61-year-old Abdul Rehman, residents of Korangi's Sector 50-C, had been in Indian custody since November 19, 2017. The released prisoners also included 35-year-old Mehboob Ali Mallah from Badin, 64-year-old Bashir from Musa Mohalla in Garski Village, Maripur, and 60-year-old Khamiso from Shah Bandar, Sujawal. They had been detained since September 22, 2023.

The spokesperson said the remaining three among the 14 released Pakistanis included a deaf and mute man from Bahawalpur who had reportedly crossed the border around 10 years ago. His family collected him from the Edhi Centre in Lahore.

Another released prisoner, a resident of Baldia Town, had spent eight years in Indian custody before his family also took him home from Lahore.

headline: 740 death-trap buildings still standing
description: 740 death-trap buildings still standing
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Karachi's building safety watchdog has come under fire after an audit by the Auditor General of Pakistan revealed that 740 declared dangerous buildings in the city remain standing, while the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA) awarded demolition contracts without ensuring that contractors possessed the necessary machinery or technical expertise. The damning report has exposed a wider pattern of regulatory lapses, questionable construction approvals, financial irregularities and administrative failures within the authority tasked with safeguarding the city's buildings.

The audit report has also questioned the effectiveness of SBCA's much-touted single-window system for construction approvals. Despite its introduction to streamline the process, the authority took an average of 50.85 days to issue construction permits, compared with just 14 days under the manual system in 2019.

The report further revealed that construction permits were issued without obtaining mandatory NOCs for sale and advertisement, potentially exposing buyers to legal complications arising from the sale of units lacking the required clearances.

headline: Sindh woos ASEAN, Portuguese for trade
description: Sindh woos ASEAN, Portuguese for trade
article_text:
From desalination plants to football coaching, Sindh is seeking to broaden its international partnerships, inviting businesses from Southeast Asia and Portugal to invest in the province and collaborate in agriculture, energy, technology, tourism and sports.

Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah extended the invitation during separate meetings with a high-level ASEAN delegation and Portuguese Ambassador to Pakistan Paulo Domingues at the Chief Minister's House on Friday.

Leading the ASEAN delegation, Philippine Ambassador Dr Emmanuel R Fernandez, who also chairs the ASEAN Committee in Islamabad, was accompanied by diplomats from Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam and Brunei Darussalam.

CM Shah urged ASEAN countries to explore investment opportunities in agriculture, food processing, pharmaceuticals, information technology, energy, minerals, industry, logistics and tourism. He said Sindh, particularly Karachi, offered investors access to a large domestic market, an established industrial base, port infrastructure and skilled manpower.

The diplomats discussed expanding bilateral trade, attracting investment and promoting cultural and educational exchanges. Murad said Pakistan and the Philippines had maintained friendly relations since establishing diplomatic ties in 1949, adding that the second session of their Joint Economic Commission, held in Manila on February 19, 2026, offered opportunities to advance trade and investment. Welcoming the Philippine ambassador's interest in raising bilateral trade to $500 million, he identified rice trade, seed development, agricultural technology, food processing, pharmaceuticals and energy as potential areas of cooperation.

In his meeting with the Portuguese ambassador, CM Shah sought international expertise to address Karachi's growing water needs, proposing that Portuguese companies specialising in desalination be linked with the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation (KWSC).

headline: BISE Lahore to begin digital marking
description: BISE Lahore to begin digital marking
author: ADNAN LODHI
article_text:
The Lahore Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE) is moving towards digital assessment of answer scripts with four subjects selected for the initial phase and an expansion expected for the examinations next year.

The development comes ahead of the Intermediate Second Annual examinations scheduled to begin on November 3, when biology, chemistry, computer science and statistics will have on-screen marking.

According to sources, the board has prepared a complete answer book and bubble sheet pattern for the computer science exam.

The board also arranged district-wise seminars and training workshops during October for educational institutions and examination personnel. The plan covers Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura and Nankana Sahib.

Under the new mechanism, students will continue to use conventional answer sheets.

However, instead of distributing the answer books among examiners for manual checking, the completed scripts will be scanned and converted into digital record before being made available through an electronic assessment platform.

Examiners will evaluate the scanned scripts on computer screens, allowing the examination authorities to monitor the allocation and assessment of answer books through a centralised mechanism.

The initial selection of four subjects provides the board an opportunity to assess the technical and administrative requirements of the system before extending it.

Education Minister Rana Sikandar Hayat had announced that manual checking would be replaced by on-screen assessment from 2027 with digital identification and QR code-based arrangements.

The government has presented the initiative as an effort to improve transparency and consistency in the evaluation.

According to experts, the digital assessment could address several weaknesses associated with paper checking.

"Physical answer books require transportation, distribution and collection, while monitoring the progress of individual examiners through the manual process can be administratively demanding.

However, electronic allocation could allow examination authorities to maintain a record of which examiner receives a particular script when its assessment begins and when the marking is completed. It could also help identify delayed assessments and discrepancies requiring attention," a BISE official said.

LAHORE:

The Lahore Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE) is moving towards digital assessment of answer scripts with four subjects selected for the initial phase and an expansion expected for the examinations next year.

The development comes ahead of the Intermediate Second Annual examinations scheduled to begin on November 3, when biology, chemistry, computer science and statistics will have on-screen marking.

According to sources, the board has prepared a complete answer book and bubble sheet pattern for the computer science exam.

The board also arranged district-wise seminars and training workshops during October for educational institutions and examination personnel. The plan covers Lahore, Kasur, Sheikhupura and Nankana Sahib.

Under the new mechanism, students will continue to use conventional answer sheets.

However, instead of distributing the answer books among examiners for manual checking, the completed scripts will be scanned and converted into digital record before being made available through an electronic assessment platform.

Examiners will evaluate the scanned scripts on computer screens, allowing the examination authorities to monitor the allocation and assessment of answer books through a centralised mechanism.

The initial selection of four subjects provides the board an opportunity to assess the technical and administrative requirements of the system before extending it.

Education Minister Rana Sikandar Hayat had announced that manual checking would be replaced by on-screen assessment from 2027 with digital identification and QR code-based arrangements.

The government has presented the initiative as an effort to improve transparency and consistency in the evaluation.

According to experts, the digital assessment could address several weaknesses associated with paper checking.

"Physical answer books require transportation, distribution and collection, while monitoring the progress of individual examiners through the manual process can be administratively demanding.

However, electronic allocation could allow examination authorities to maintain a record of which examiner receives a particular script when its assessment begins and when the marking is completed. It could also help identify delayed assessments and discrepancies requiring attention," a BISE official said.
